title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.
status_note: The source asks for a broad characterization. This card explicitly fixes an effective separable streaming variant rather than attributing every resource convention to the source. The 2016 one-variable result is only a partial classification, and the later metric counterexample concerns another model. No full characterization for the specified domain was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

progress.text: Guha and Indyk pose the broad distance-sketchability question and discuss separable coordinate costs.
Braverman and coauthors classify nearly all one-variable frequency aggregates and explicitly identify the result as a partial answer for difference-based dissimilarities.
Khot and Naor show that the norm-sketchability characterization does not extend to arbitrary metrics.

importance.reason: A unifying classification problem for streaming dissimilarity estimation, extending both norm-based geometry and the known one-variable aggregation framework.

sentences: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates.
The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative.
The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations.
The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs.
Known offset obstructions, difference-based aggregate classifications and norm-sketching results cover only parts of this domain.

definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.
